description: 4 attacking challenges for White in the Keres Attack. Launch the g4-g5 pawn storm after 8.Rg1 — break with g5, sacrifice on e6, and swing the rook to h3.

drills.briefExplanation: g5! cracks Black's kingside after the central break. After hxg5 hxg5, Be7 is forced and Qe2+ seizes the initiative.
drills.description: Black strikes with d5 in the center, but White's kingside attack arrives first. Blast open the h-file with g5 and follow up with Qe2+.
drills.explanation: When Black plays the critical 8...d5, the position opens in the center — but the Keres Attack was designed for exactly this. After 9.exd5 Nxd5 10.Nxd5 exd5, White ignores the center and plays 11.g5! The point: Black's h6-pawn must take (11...hxg5), and after 12.hxg5 the h-file is blasted open with Black's king still in the center. Black scrambles with 12...Be7, developing and preparing to castle, but White strikes first with 13.Qe2+! — the check forces Black's king to move or block, and White's initiative is overwhelming: the open h-file, the advanced g5-pawn cramping Black's kingside, and the knight on d4 dominating the center. This is the Keres Attack dream — Black's central counter is met not with defense but with a faster flank attack.
drills.name: The g5 Break

drills.briefExplanation: h5 and g5 build the pawn steamroller. After Nh7, g6! wedges a pawn into Black's kingside and threatens to shatter the pawn cover.
drills.description: Against Black's slow setup, launch the pawn storm with h5. Keep pushing with g5, and when the knight retreats, wedge with g6.
drills.explanation: When Black develops quietly with 8...Bd7, White has time for the full Keres pawn storm. The move 9.h5! is the start — White gains space and prepares g5, and Black cannot easily stop the avalanche. After 9...Be7 10.g5, Black's kingside is under siege: the g5-pawn attacks h6, the h5-pawn is ready to advance, and Black's pieces are passively placed. Black retreats 10...Nh7, but White plays the crushing 11.g6! This pawn wedge is the thematic Keres breakthrough — the g6-pawn attacks f7, threatens gxf7+ forking king and rook, and paralyzes Black's kingside. Black cannot take (11...fxg6 12.hxg6 wins the h7-knight), and White's attack plays itself: Qe2, Bd3, and O-O-O with a decisive initiative. The h5+g5+g6 steamroller is why the Keres Attack scores so well in practice — Black's Scheveningen setup is too slow to meet it.
drills.name: Pawn Storm

drills.briefExplanation: Nxe6! demolishes Black's pawn cover. After fxe6, Qe2 centralizes with threats — Black's king will never find safety.
drills.description: With Black's knight driven to h7, sacrifice on e6 to rip open the center. After fxe6, bring the queen to e2 with a raging initiative.
drills.explanation: This is the Keres Attack's signature sacrifice. After 8...a6 9.g5 hxg5 10.hxg5 Nh7, Black's kingside looks solid — but White plays the stunning 11.Nxe6! The knight sacrifice demolishes Black's central pawn cover: after 11...fxe6 (forced, as 11...dxe6?? drops the d6-pawn and 11...Qe7 12.Nxg7+ wins), Black's e6-pawn is gone, the f-file is half-open toward Black's king, and the dark squares around e8 are fatally weakened. White follows with 12.Qe2!, centralizing the queen with multiple threats: Qh5+ is coming, the g5-pawn cramps Black's kingside, and Black's king is stuck in the center with no safe haven. The e6-square is the Scheveningen's Achilles heel — the pawn on e6 is the linchpin of Black's entire setup, and removing it by force collapses the position. This sacrifice appears in countless Keres Attack masterpieces.
drills.name: The e6 Sacrifice

drills.briefExplanation: Rg3! begins the rook lift — the rook will swing to h3 for a direct kingside assault. After O-O, Rh3 eyes h6 and Black's king.
drills.description: Start the famous rook lift with Rg3. When Black castles into the storm, swing to h3 and keep attacking with g5.
drills.explanation: The rook lift is the Keres Attack's most visually striking idea. From g1, the rook has a highway to the kingside: 10.Rg3! prepares to swing to h3, where it will join the pawn storm in a direct assault on Black's king. Black's most natural reply is 10...O-O, castling by hand — but this walks into the attack, as the h6-pawn is now a target. White plays 11.Rh3!, and suddenly Black faces a rook, two advanced pawns, and soon a queen all aimed at the kingside. After 11...Re8 (defending e6 and preparing to run), White continues 12.g5! — the pawn storm resumes with the rook already in place on h3. The g1-g3-h3 maneuver is a hallmark of modern attacking chess: the rook, normally a slow piece to activate, becomes the star attacker in just two moves. Fischer and Kasparov both used this lift to demolish Scheveningen setups.
drills.name: Rook Lift
